[...] O acento primário recai sempre na penúltima sílaba, exceto quando a última sílaba tiver duas moras ou, em outros termos, for uma sílaba pesada (ver exemplos 1 e 2). [p. 160] (4) O acento primário ocorrerá sempre na penúltima sílaba da palavra (a), exceto se (b) a última sílaba contiver duas moras (isto é, duas vogais ou uma vogal nasal [...] a. σ→'σ / _σ# b. σ→'σ / _#]{VV, V} [p. 161]
new_statements.translation: The Apurinã language presents a predictable stress pattern, hence it does not mark lexical distinctions. [...] Primary stress always falls on the penultimate syllable, except when the last syllable has two moras or, in other terms, is a heavy syllable (see examples 1 and 2). [p. 160] (4) Primary stress will always occur on the penultimate syllable of the word (a), except if (b) the last syllable contains two moras (that is, two vowels or a nasal vowel [...] [p. 161]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Apurinã (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule, so this source supplies the placement: penultimate default with final stress when the final syllable is bimoraic (weight-sensitive), plus alternating secondary stress. Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is predictable (non-contrastive): on the penultimate syllable by default, but on the final syllable when that syllable is bimoraic (long vowel, diphthong/VV, or a nasal vowel, which behaves as heavy). Monosyllables must be bimoraic (minimal-word constraint, p. 161). Left-headed (trochaic) feet. Examples: ['pãma] 'pama fruit', [tso'pata] 'cockroach' (penult); [ki'kiʋ] 'garden', [tse'rĩi] 'tooth' (final heavy). The authors follow Facundes (2000).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 161: 'Como descreve Facundes (2000), além do acento primário, a língua Apurinã ainda possui acentos secundários, que ocorrem sempre nas sílabas pares e "deslocam-se" para a esquerda da sílaba com acento primário.' p. 162: secondary stress occurs in words of more than three syllables, on every second syllable counting leftward from the primary stress (e.g. [ˌtaka'tarɨ], [aˌnãpa'narɨ], [ˌapaˌrɨ̃gaˌʋati'nĩã]). Acoustically, duration distinguishes primary from secondary stress but not secondary from unstressed (pp. 164-166).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the last syllable is heavy (VV, long vowel, or nasal vowel); nasal vowels count as bimoraic, which the authors flag as a theoretical puzzle (pp. 160-161). No lexical exceptions mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Santos & Facundes 2015 and Santos 2013 describe Apurinã of the Purus river communities (SE Amazonas), data from a small number of speakers (2015: one speaker analysed out of three recorded); no dialect is named. Ishida 2025 treats geographic variation among 18 localities but only in segments. The catalog entry 'Apurinã' is a bare name with no rule and no dialect.

new_statements.quote: Apurinã é uma língua de acento predizível, e como toda língua que possui acento fixo na penúltima sílaba, esse elemento prosódico não possui status fonêmico. [pp. 24-25] Além disso, o tipo de regra de alternância do acento em apurinã é o da sensibilidade quantitativa, aquela que afirma que toda sílaba pesada (i.e., bimoraica) é elegível a receber o acento. [p. 26] Palavras dissilábicas são paroxítonas, exceto se a última sílaba for pesada [p. 26] Palavras polissilábicas são paroxítonas, exceto se a última sílaba for pesada. Palavras paroxítonas com 4-5 sílabas (97-110) apresentam um acento secundário na quarta sílaba (da direita para a esquerda), e paroxítonas com 6-7 sílabas (111-120) apresentam um acento secundário nas quarta e sexta sílabas [p. 27]
new_statements.translation: Apurinã is a language with predictable stress, and as in every language that has fixed stress on the penultimate syllable, this prosodic element has no phonemic status. [pp. 24-25] Moreover, the type of stress-alternation rule in Apurinã is the quantity-sensitive one, which states that every heavy (i.e. bimoraic) syllable is eligible to receive stress. [p. 26] Disyllabic words are paroxytone (penult-stressed), unless the last syllable is heavy [p. 26] Polysyllabic words are paroxytone, unless the last syllable is heavy. Paroxytone words with 4-5 syllables (97-110) show a secondary stress on the fourth syllable (from right to left), and paroxytones with 6-7 syllables (111-120) show secondary stress on the fourth and sixth syllables [p. 27]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable and non-phonemic. Default penultimate stress for disyllables, trisyllables and longer words; final stress when the final syllable is heavy (bimoraic: long vowel, diphthong, nasal vowel), e.g. ku.ˈkuj 'eagle', ju.ˈtsãː 'to sew', e.ˈnẽː 'to grow'. Monosyllables must be heavy (minimal word, p. 26). The pattern is analysed as moraic trochees, left-headed (p. 28), following Facundes (2000).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 25: primary stress plus secondary stresses 'que se deslocam para a esquerda em posições alternadas' (that shift leftward in alternating positions). p. 27: secondary stress on the 4th syllable from the right in 4-5-syllable paroxytones, and on the 4th and 6th in 6-7-syllable words. Acoustic chapters (pp. 32-52) test duration, F0 and intensity for primary vs secondary vs unstressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final syllable is heavy (pp. 26-27); no lexical exceptions listed. The p. 25 phrase 'acento fixo na penúltima sílaba' is a loose summary that the thesis's own rule (penult unless final heavy) qualifies.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge: final if heavy = nasal V or diphthong, else penult; heavy antepenults ignored; alternating secondary stress leftward) rests on the standard 674-pp reference grammar (Facundes 2000), which we hold; the deciding quotation was re-located verbatim at the cited sections/pages in the text we hold. A Crossref search (92 'Apurinã' records) and the UFPA repository turned up the only later stress-specific literature — Santos 2013 (acoustic MA thesis) and Santos & Facundes 2015 (instrumental article) — both downloaded to and both restate the same rule (penult, except bimoraic final = VV/diphthong or any nasal vowel) and add that duration is the correlate of primary stress; Ishida 2025 (phonological variation monograph, downloaded via its DOI) is silent on stress. WALS 14A-17A independently code the language the same
